# 1. Data Structure Summary & Initial Exploration

## 1.1 Subset the Data

**Write code to create the subset `jan_feb_flights` below:**

```{r subset-data}
jan_feb_flights <- flights %>%
  filter(month %in% c(1, 2))
```

## 1.2 Column Overview

Explore the columns in `jan_feb_flights`.
Which are numeric, which are categorical/text/factor?  
Are there missing values?

```{r}
# explore the types of the columns in jan_feb_flights
glimpse(jan_feb_flights)
```

```{r}
# which columns are integer
jan_feb_flights %>% select(where(is.integer)) %>% names()

# which columns are double
jan_feb_flights %>% select(where(is.double)) %>% names()

# which columns are character
jan_feb_flights %>% select(where(is.character)) %>% names()
```

```{r}
# which columns contain NA's (named columns, using summarise and is.na)
jan_feb_flights %>%
  summarise(
    dep_time_na  = sum(is.na(dep_time)),
    dep_delay_na = sum(is.na(dep_delay)),
    arr_time_na  = sum(is.na(arr_time)),
    arr_delay_na = sum(is.na(arr_delay)),
    air_time_na  = sum(is.na(air_time)),
    tailnum_na   = sum(is.na(tailnum))
  )

# alternative that checks every column at once (suggested by GenAI)
colSums(is.na(jan_feb_flights))
```

**Summary:**  

The integer columns are year, month, day, dep_time, sched_dep_time, arr_time, sched_arr_time, flight and hour. The double columns are dep_delay, arr_delay, air_time, distance and minute. The character columns are carrier, tailnum, origin and dest. time_hour is a date-time, so it is neither numeric nor character. (Check these lists against your own output.) Missing values appear in dep_time, dep_delay, arr_time, arr_delay, air_time and tailnum: [paste the counts from your output]. The missing departure values are mostly cancelled flights, and the missing arrival values are cancelled and diverted flights.

# 2. Delays & Weather

**Goal:** Analyze relationship between average departure delay and wind gust speed.

## 2.1 Code

```{r eval=TRUE} 
# join the datasets
jan_feb_flights <- jan_feb_flights %>%
  left_join(weather, by = c("origin", "year", "month", "day", "hour")) 
```

```{r}
# is there a difference in wind speed when wind_gust is missing vs not missing?
jan_feb_flights %>%
  group_by(gust_missing = is.na(wind_gust)) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_wind_speed = mean(wind_speed, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_wind_speed = sd(wind_speed, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Describe the difference in wind speed when wind_gust is missing vs not missing:

[Fill in using your output.] Mean wind speed is [X] when wind_gust is missing and [Y] when it is recorded. Gusts are normally only reported when the wind is strong enough, so wind speed is higher when a gust is recorded.

```{r eval=TRUE} 
# create a new variable, gust_present
jan_feb_flights <- jan_feb_flights %>%
  mutate(gust_present = !is.na(wind_gust))
```


```{r}
# is there a relationship between gust_present and dep_delay?
jan_feb_flights %>%
  group_by(gust_present) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_dep_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_dep_delay = sd(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Describe the relationship between gust_present and dep_delay you see (if any).

[Fill in using your output.] The mean departure delay is [X] minutes when gusts are recorded and [Y] minutes when they are not, a difference of [Z] minutes. The standard deviations are large ([values]) relative to that gap, so the two groups overlap a lot. This shows an association only, not that gusts cause delays. Flights with no matching weather record also count as gust_present = FALSE, which may affect the comparison.

# 3. Bootstrap confidence intervals

## 3.1 Bootstrap CI using `infer`

```{r}
# focus on flights departing from JFK with non-missing dep_delay
jfk_flights <- jan_feb_flights %>%
 filter(origin == "JFK", !is.na(dep_delay))
```


```{r eval=TRUE} 
# Compute the sample mean
mean_dep_delay <- jfk_flights %>% summarise(mean_jfk = mean(dep_delay)) %>% pull(mean_jfk)

# Construct bootstrap distribution
set.seed(99)  # for reproducibility
boot_dist <- jfk_flights %>%
  specify(response = dep_delay) %>%
  generate(reps = 1500, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat = "mean")                 

# Compute 95% confidence interval (percentile method)
boot_dist %>%
  summarise(lower = quantile(stat, 0.025),
            upper = quantile(stat, 0.975))
```

The instructions also ask for the mean departure delay for flights with and without gusts recorded. This repeats the same bootstrap separately for each group:

```{r eval=TRUE}
set.seed(99)
boot_gust <- jfk_flights %>%
  filter(gust_present) %>%
  specify(response = dep_delay) %>%
  generate(reps = 1500, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat = "mean")

boot_no_gust <- jfk_flights %>%
  filter(!gust_present) %>%
  specify(response = dep_delay) %>%
  generate(reps = 1500, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat = "mean")

boot_gust %>%
  summarise(group = "gust recorded",
            lower = quantile(stat, 0.025), upper = quantile(stat, 0.975))
boot_no_gust %>%
  summarise(group = "no gust recorded",
            lower = quantile(stat, 0.025), upper = quantile(stat, 0.975))
```

**Interpretation for the confidence interval**:

[Fill in your numbers.] We are 95% confident that the true mean departure delay for JFK flights in January and February is between [lower] and [upper] minutes. For the gust comparison, the interval for flights with gusts is [..] to [..] and without gusts is [..] to [..]. [If the intervals overlap, say the data do not clearly show a difference; if they do not overlap, say the data suggest a real difference in mean delay.]

## 3.2 Using base R

The following code achieves the same using base R and a for loop. 
Ask GenAI to explain how it works and discuss it with the group. Then find a tutor, and try to explain them what you did or didn't understand.


```{r eval=TRUE} 
set.seed(99)
n <- nrow(jfk_flights)
B <- 1500       
boot_means2 <- numeric(B)

for (i in 1:B) {
  idx <- sample(n, replace = TRUE)
  boot_means2[i] <- mean(jfk_flights$dep_delay[idx])
}

hist(boot_means2, breaks = 30, main = "Bootstrap means (for loop)", xlab = "Mean Departure Delay")
ci2_lower <- quantile(boot_means2, 0.025)
ci2_upper <- quantile(boot_means2, 0.975)

mean_dep_delay; ci2_lower; ci2_upper
```

What the loop does: `n` is the sample size, `B` is the number of resamples, and `boot_means2` is an empty vector to store the results. Each pass of the loop draws `n` row numbers with replacement (`sample(n, replace = TRUE)`), takes the mean of the departure delays for those rows, and stores it in position `i`. After 1500 repeats, the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the stored means give the 95% confidence interval. (The workshop instructions print `mean_arr_delay`, but that object does not exist here, so `mean_dep_delay` is used.)

## 3.3 Reflection

[Edit so it matches what you actually did.] The explanation of the loop was clear line by line, especially that `sample(n, replace = TRUE)` is the resampling step. The infer and base R intervals should be very close but may differ slightly because the random draws differ. I checked this by comparing the two intervals. [Add whether the tutor's explanation matched, and whether you needed to re-prompt.]

# 4. Airline Delay Analysis

**Goal:** For each airline, what are the mean and median arrival delays in Jan/Feb? Which is the worst on average?

```{r eval=TRUE} 
# Join jan_feb_flights with airlines by carrier code
jan_feb_flights <- jan_feb_flights %>%
  left_join(airlines, by = "carrier")
```


```{r wrangling1}
# Group by airline, summarize n, mean and median arrival delay
# Arrange descending by mean delay
jan_feb_flights %>%
  group_by(carrier, name) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_arr_delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_arr_delay = median(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_arr_delay))
```

**Which airline(s) had the highest mean? Is there anything notable about the worst airline?**

[Fill in using the top row of your table.] The airline with the highest mean arrival delay is [name] with a mean of [X] minutes and a median of [Y] minutes, based on [n] flights. [Comment on whether n is small compared with the other airlines, and whether the mean is much higher than the median, which would mean a few very long delays pull the average up.]

## 4.1 Reflection

[Edit so it matches what you actually did.] Claude helped with the join and with the group_by/summarise structure. Things to watch for: running the airlines join twice creates duplicate `name.x`/`name.y` columns, and `na.rm = TRUE` is needed or every mean is NA. # 5. GenAI Use Reflection

[Edit this section after discussing with your team. These are draft points.]

- **Risks of GenAI for coding:** it can produce code that looks right but is wrong or does not match what you have covered, and it can state things confidently without being correct. The workshop instructions themselves contained a mismatch (`mean_arr_delay` vs `mean_dep_delay`), so checking against your own output matters. I used Claude directly, not IDS-sidekick.
- **Risks of copying code verbatim:** you do not learn the concept, you cannot debug it when it breaks, and you may not notice mistakes.
- **Learner vs proficient coder:** a learner cannot easily tell whether the output is correct and may use functions not yet taught; an experienced coder can spot errors quickly and uses GenAI to save time.
- **Attempting first:** trying first makes your questions more specific, and the feedback more useful because you can compare it with your own approach.
- **GenAI as navigator vs code generator:** a navigator that asks questions and explains concepts supports learning better than one that hands over code. [Add your view of IDS-sidekick.]
- **One insight each:** [each team member adds one tip, for example: run the code and check the output yourself, and ask for the simplest version using only what you have been taught.]
